history: Classical Latin had a serious verb for speaking: loqui. Ordinary Romans preferred something livelier, fabulari, ‘to chat, to tell stories’, from fabula, ‘a tale’. That is the verb Portuguese inherited. The middle of the word wore away, and fabulare became falar. Spanish took the same verb but turned the f into h: hablar. Portuguese kept its f, so a Portuguese speaker falas and a Spanish one hablas. French and Italian took a different verb again, parler and parlare, from the Church word for a story told in parables. The family of fabula is still easy to see in Portuguese: fábula, ‘fable’, and fala, ‘speech’, as in a fala do Porto, ‘the way people speak in Porto’.
historyEinfach: Falar means ‘to speak’. It comes from Latin fabulari, ‘to chat, to tell stories’. The Latin word fabula means ‘story’. Spanish hablar comes from the same verb: Spanish changed f into h. Portuguese kept the f.

elsewhere.text: Old Spanish still wrote fablar; later the f became an h, and today the h is silent.
French also turned ‘telling stories’ into ‘speaking’, but with a different story word.
